chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Hareez, from Muhammad ibn Muslim who said:
I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a slaughtered animal slaughtered toward other than the Qibla. He said: Eat, and there is no problem with that, as long as it was not intentional.

He said: And I asked him about a man who slaughtered and did not say the Name (Bismillah). He said: If he had forgotten, then let him say the Name when he remembers, saying: In the Name of God upon its beginning and upon its ending.

key_terms.الْقِبْلَة: The Qibla — the direction of the Kaaba in Mecca, toward which Muslims face in prayer and ritual slaughter
key_terms.ذَبِيحَة: A slaughtered/sacrificed animal; the act and product of ritual slaughter (dhabiha)
key_terms.نَاسِياً: One who has forgotten; forgetfulness (nisyan) as a legal excuse in Islamic jurisprudence
key_terms.يَتَعَمَّدْهُ: To do deliberately/intentionally; the legal concept of intent ('amd) as a criterion in rulings
key_terms.يُسَمِّي: To say the Name, i.e., to pronounce Bismillah; the required invocation at slaughter

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to eat an animal slaughtered away from the Qibla or without saying Bismillah?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) was asked two questions about slaughtering: (1) regarding an animal slaughtered away from the Qibla direction — the Imam ruled it permissible to eat as long as the deviation was not intentional; (2) regarding omitting the Bismillah at slaughter — the Imam ruled that if forgotten, saying it upon remembrance (covering both the beginning and end of the slaughter) suffices. These rulings reflect a core jurisprudential principle: that inadvertent acts do not carry the same legal consequences as deliberate violations, showing leniency toward forgetfulness in acts of worship.
